newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices drop as storm worries ease, gold surges.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices drop as storm worries ease, gold surges.

text.p: Oil prices fell sharply on Friday as fears faded that a hurricane in the Gulf of Mexico would disrupt refinery operations.
In other markets, gold prices rose for a second day as speculators continued to take profits after recent heavy selling and grain prices rose on forecats of dry weather for the Midwest.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for August delivery closed 72 cents a barrel lower at $19.27.
Hurricane Danny, packing maximum sustained winds of 75 miles per hour, moved northeast through the Gulf over the tip of Louisiana at a slow pace on Friday.
The National Weather Service said the storm could dump up to 20 inches of rain in some parts of the coast from Mississippi to Florida but would weaken on Saturday.
Texaco Inc. said it was returning 365 workers to 10 rigs in the Gulf after evacuating them on Thursday, and operations were seen returning to normal during the weekend.
Mobil Corp. expected production would be back up by the weekend at six offshore fields shut Thursday, while Exxon Corp. said it had suffered only a minor production loss.
"Workers were returning to work following the hurricane and that also led to some (sell) stops being touched on the way down," said Rick Navy, broker with Paribas Futures Inc. in New York.
"There was little belief in crude when it stood above $20.00, so prices looked overbought," added Navy.
Oil prices, led by gasoline, had risen on Thursday on concerns about disrupted product supplies from the growing strom in the Gulf.
August heating oil ended off 1.67 cents at 52.22 cents a gallon while August gasoline finished 1.84 cents a gallon lower at 60.05 cents.
Gold prices, meanwhile, rose to the highest level in nearly two weeks as speculators who had been selling heavily in recent weeks continued to buy back futures contracts to take profits.
August delivery gold at the COMEX ended up $4.90 an ounce at $329.60, after seeing an 11-day high at $330.90.

"The slump in the stock market Friday might be used as an excuse for gold's recovery, but really it was just that funds are taking the opportunity to cover their large short positions," said Merrill Lynch commodity research director Bill O'Neill, adding that some gold producers had also been lightening up on their "short" or selling positions.
"However, our view is that this is a natural trading turn in the market but may not be a major trend change, and the 12-year lows seen last week may yet be revisited," he said.

Gold was fixed at a 12-year low in London last week at $315.75 after news of a sale of 167 metric tons of gold by the Reserve Bank of Australia, which encouraged massive amounts of extra short selling by hedge funds, analysts said.
Buoyed by gold, September silver ended up 2.5 cents at $4.270 an ounce, recovering from a break to life-of-contract lows this week at $4.1450.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn and soybean prices closed higher on forecasts for continued dry weather in parched portions of central Illinois, a key growing area. Prices had fallen a day earlier on forecasts that spillover rains from Hurricane Danny would extend north to Illinois.
Corn for post-harvest delivery in December closed 5-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $2.54 and soybeans for November delivery closed 6-3/4 cents a bushel higher at $6.07-1/2.

"It's all weather-related," said Bill Biedermann, director of research for Allendale Inc. "We're suffering out here, there's no question about it. If we don't get rain this weekend or Monday we'll be sharply higher."
